utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everybody in and around the courtroom. This is case IT-08-91-T, the Prosecutor versus Mico Stanisic and Stojan Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Good morning to everyone. Before I take the appearances, I note the presence this morning of Ms. Korner, and I take the opportunity on behalf of the Trial Chamber to convey our condolences to her on the recent passing of her father. Yes. May we have the appearances, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Joanna Korner, Thomas Hannis, and Gramsci Di Fazio, and Crispian Smith for the Prosecution this morning. I'm only here temporarily, but may I thank you very much for the kind expression from the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. For the Stanisic Defence team, Slobodan Cvijetic, Tatjana Savic, and Deirdre Montgomery.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Dragan Krgovic, and Aleksandar Aleksic appearing for Zupljanin Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. We have been alerted that there is a concern, if I could use as vague a word as I could think of, that the Defence has in respect of an upcoming witness. Well, Ms. Korner was on her feet. Who wants to go first on this matter?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I was going to say, this is the Defence -- I'm on my feet, but I was simply, in case Your Honours haven't been alerted, going to say that there's been an e-mail exchange which I hope has been copied to Your Honours and I understand it's a Defence application, which the Prosecution, I say immediately, resists.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we hear the application. Unless, of course, there's been a change of mind, in which case we can move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour, we did not change our minds. Our application is short and very clear. Lately, and not only with this last witness, ST-163, but earlier witnesses as well, we were in a situation to have disclosed to us just before the witness's appearance voluminous material from the OTP that we have difficulty reviewing in time for cross-examination. And, again, for this witness, we received material over 270 pages in transcript, so it was impossible to study this material properly and prepare well for cross-examination. For that reason, and for the reasons I stated yesterday, and with the tempo we are working at in the courtroom, I think we should postpone this witness for a time that would allow us to prepare properly for his cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, as far as the Zupljanin Defence is concerned, the witness we are discussing relates mostly to Mr. Stanisic. But we haven't had the opportunity to see this material, so we can only support the request made by Mr. Cvijetic. We have not had occasion, as I said, to see this material overnight, but we understand it's very large.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: We are, of course, aware of the substance of the OTP's position from the e-mail exchange that we would have seen. But could, Ms. Korner, we have, for the record, the Prosecution's response to this application?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Certainly. Your Honours, the Defence made a request very recently while I was absent for disclosure under the Rule 66(B) of, effectively, any interview that we had conducted with -- when I say "we," the OTP, over the years had conducted with members of the RS MUP, regardless of whether they were relevant or not to any issue that could be seen. During the course of those searches, it transpired that although the two interviews which were disclosed yesterday are not with members of the RS MUP, they are with people who were interviewed by the OTP some years ago. And the witness who is about to testify, testified in the State Court in Bosnia and Herzegovina against those two people who have subsequently been convicted, named Ratko Lalovic and somebody with the exceedingly unlikely name of Soniboj - and I mean Soniboj - Skelaljic [phoen], who were wardens of Kula prison, which is not in the indictment. The searches showed that the next witness got a mention, not surprisingly, because he dealt in his position with these two men. And so as I said in the e-mail, effectively, in the spirit of total cooperation, even though it doesn't strictly fall under the nature of the request that was made, and out of an abundance of caution, we disclosed those two interviews. I have provided to the Defence the references where this man appears, the page numbers. Out of the so-called 279 pages, in one interview he receives references on 13 of those pages and in the other, 14. And the references - can I just give Your Honours one example, please - they are largely that he signed various documents, which is not a matter which is going to be in dispute and, indeed, was raised with an earlier witness. And if I can take this -- this is page 77 of the interview with Soniboj, that on the 15th of November the witness - for the moment I'm not mentioning his name, although I don't believe he has protective measures - brought me the decision, namely, that he was appointed governor. And it's small sentences like that. Your Honours, we say there is absolutely no reason why this witness's evidence should be adjourned. For some reason, I don't know why, at the moment, the Defence are making attempts to delay almost all major witnesses. Ewan Brown has already now been moved to January. And we say, without giving proper reasons for why out of this, I think, one, two, three -- five lawyers they have working on the Stanisic team, and I believe it's one, two, three, four on the Zupljanin team, they cannot look at those references to see whether it affects any cross-examination of the witness. And that's our position. Who is here and ready to go.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Does the -- does the Defence wish to respond to what Ms. Korner has had to say?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours, briefly. The Defence cannot use the references chosen by the Prosecution. The Defence is entitled to prepare its cross-examination in keeping with their own strategy, their own tactics, and to determine themselves what they will use out of each and every document. So we have to study the entire material, and then it is up to us to decide what references are apt to be used for cross-examination. I, therefore, believe that the arguments presented by Ms. Korner do not stand and cannot be helpful in preparing for our work. But Ms. Korner said something else that opens up another issue that I wanted to raise; namely, I thought I would suggest that the OTP not question that witness about the circumstances in Kula if that is not an issue here. However, Ms. Korner says that she will have to deal with that issue, particularly because of the fact that the persons whose statements have been disclosed to us held posts in that correctional facility of Kula. One was a warden; another was a deputy. So they are very relevant to the events in Kula. So if the Prosecution can guarantee that they will steer clear of this issue, then we can -- we can drop this objection. We are prepared to do the same.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Well, of course, the Chamber has no comment on the last half of Mr. Cvijetic's reply. It's -- it's entirely a matter for the side calling the witness as to what -- having -- subject, of course, to the rules of relevance, what evidence they lead. As for the first part of his reply, we entirely agree with Mr. Cvijetic's observation that it is not for the -- in this case, the Prosecution, to determine what may or may not be relevant to the Defence in the presentation of its case. However, we are not satisfied that the material which the Defence would have recently been referred to is of such ex facie relevance as to require that the calling of this witness be delayed. Indeed, we would presume to add that the nature of advocacy often requires, in terms of preparation for court, a continual adjustment to new factors. And in this case, new facts have come to the attention of the -- of counsel, and it is, of course, not for us to presume to tell counsel how to divide up the work. But the -- as I said, we see no reason to delay the appearance of the witness, and counsel would have to decide how best to deal with this. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, thank you very much. And I'll leave the court, if I may, to Mr. Di Fazio and Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Yes, before the witness comes in, I would wish to correct an indication that I gave yesterday which was erroneous on my part, namely, that we had already admitted Ms. Tabeau's reports into evidence. This obviously was not quite so because we have already ruled that we will not admit the expert reports until after her testimony, at the end of her testimony. So with this little correction for which I apologise, we are ready to continue with the witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, Mr. Di Fazio -- I've -- I heard him saying that's entirely understood. We understand the position with the expert's reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. May I proceed, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, please. The -- I would remind the witness, Ms. Tabeau, that you're still, of course, on your oath. Yes, Mr. Di Fazio.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Dr. Tabeau, I just want to quickly wrap up the issue of your expertise. Yesterday the Trial Chamber asked you a number of questions about testimony you've provided, and I'm going to shortly introduce a document that will, I think, bring that up to date. But your expertise is fully laid out in the Milosevic report, I believe, and I'm not going to go through it chapter and verse; there's just a few things I want to highlight. You have a doctorate in mathematical demography, I believe?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Incidentally, the -- your expertise and your background is set out in Annex D of the Milosevic report, I believe?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is in Annex D.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes. And some of the matters concerning your past expertise and work include these: You've worked now for, I think, well over a decade or almost a decade in the Demographics Unit of the OTP?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, ten years.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And before that you worked at the Dutch National Demographic Institute for about nine years?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: At the time of the Milosevic report, I believe you'd -- you had by then authored about 90 research papers and analytical expert reports. Has that figure now changed?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course. It is now approximately 150 research papers, articles, books, expert reports. Well, we are ten years further. And when we speak about expert reports, I have presented so far approximately 40 such reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Can the witness be shown 65 ter 10396, please. 10396.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Just cast your eye over that. Is that a list of expert reports that you've prepared in various cases at the ICTY?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. These are -- this is a selection of these reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Could we have the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: That's the continuation of that list.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This list does not contain the latest reports, like the reports I prepared for the Karadzic case, for other cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: How many are missing, would you say?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Approximately ten, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I see. Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And finally, the last page.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And does that represent a more recent and more up-to-date list of cases in which you have testified as an expert?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. These are the testimonies I yesterday missed, for instance, my testimony in Seselj, in Prlic, in Perisic. So here is the whole list of the testimonies.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Okay. Thanks for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And if Your Honours please, I seek to tender that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The exhibit number will be P1622 in order to fill the gap from yesterday, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Okay. Let's get back to the reports themselves. We mentioned yesterday that there were three principal reports that we're going to discuss. And it's clear from your reports that you've used various sets of numbers or statistics in preparation of those reports. Are the principle sets of statistics that you use or did use to produce the reports basically these: The 1991 census conducted in Bosnia; the 1997 and 1998 voters' registration for elections in Bosnia; and, finally, 12 databases dealing with deaths and victims of war that you obtained from various organs and institutions in Bosnia? Are they the basic three sets of statistics that you used?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's the case. And I rather call them statistical sources, not statistics. These are sources that we used to make statistics that are discussed in our reports. I want to make a point: All these sources are individual-level sources. They are composed of individual records, records representing persons. So we work with individual data and not with aggregate statistics. We occasionally do use some aggregate statistics compiled by others, and this is done mainly for context to our purposes. But as a matter of fact, we use individual-level sources, based on which we compile our own statistics. And these sources you mentioned are the major sources, not all of them, major sources that we used for making our reports presented in this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's focus on the census, please. You -- in your report, and particularly in the Milosevic report, you provide a lot of detail of how the census itself was conducted. You make the comment at page 5 of the report that in statistical practice population census is the largest and most complete source of information about the population in a country. You stand by that?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course. There are also other systems, especially in developed country, western countries, in which there is no census at all. But we are speaking of countries that have enough means to establish individual population registers. In such situation, data is collected systematically and kept in a central register from which any statistics can be made. In countries like the former Yugoslavia where there was no central register, population register, the population census is the source, the most important, most complete source, of information about the population. Censuses were made every ten years. The last census, before the war started, was in 1991, March 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Incidentally, there's the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Di Fazio, before you go on, at line 6 in the transcript -- page 10, line 6, I thought I heard the witness "aggregate statistics." What appears is "aggravate statistics." Could you clarify this with her, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Can you -- you've heard His Honour's question --

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Clarify that, please.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Aggregate. Aggregate statistics, not aggravate. Aggregate statistics.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: What precisely are aggregate statistics?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Aggregate statistics are numbers presented for group data, for instance, the size of population is an example of such an aggregate statistics. This number is obtained obviously from counting individual records representing different persons in a population.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you for that. In your -- in the Milosevic report, you provide a lot of detail concerning the organisation and mechanics of the actual census, and I believe you discuss matters such as the laws regulating the conduct of the census, the organs in Bosnia that actually did conduct the census, and the training and methods used by census workers, including the interviewers or enumerators. Are they all discussed at Annex B3 of the Milosevic report?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is correct. This information was provided to me by a person who participated in the conduct of the 1991 census in Bosnia and Herzegovina. It was a person who actually, years long, was involved in the preparations, also methodological presentations of the census. She was part of the republican and also federal commissions, census commissions, for this census.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Okay. You also talk about issue, in the Milosevic report, about the quality control that was adopted in -- in Bosnia for the actual census itself. There's only one aspect that I want to you explain to the Court and that is the pilot census that was conducted in Bosnia. Can you please explain to the Court what the pilot census was and what -- what they are and what -- what effect that has on the quality of the statistical source?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Pilot census is usually done a few years before the actual census. In Bosnia, this pilot census took place in 1988. It is a census based on the actual census questionnaire which is distributed by the census enumerators in a small number of census enumeration areas. As far as I remember, there were probably eight municipalities in which a random sample of enumeration areas was selected for the pilot. So the main purpose of the pilot census is to test the census questionnaire and to test the behaviour of interviewers, coding practices, organisational issues. Based on the results of the pilot census, still there is enough time to make changes in the actual procedures that will be applied later in the actual census. So that was the main purpose of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: And it was done in Bosnia, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. Please explain now to the Trial Chamber the process that occurred with the statistical source census from the point of time when the interviewer went to the household, spoke to the person, took down the information and wrote it in his form, to the point of time when it was received by you, the OTP Demographics Unit.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is again only one part in the long chain of activities related to the completion of the census. But anyway, the interviewers went to see all households in their census enumeration areas. The census enumeration areas are small geographic areas which covered the entire country. Every interviewer had a number of them falling under his or her responsibility. And in this region comprising a number of small enumeration areas, this person was taking the interviews and was responsible for covering all households living in this territory. So once the interviews were completed, the interviewer had to check the questionnaires, how complete they were, coded answers whenever necessary; and once his or her own checks were done, the interviewer provided the material to the municipal instructor, census instructor, who, again, was supposed to check the completeness of the material from this given interviewer, in terms of the coverage in terms of completion of the census questionnaires. Once the material was accepted, there were cases that interviewers had to reiterate their efforts and make improvements in the materials they provided, but at some point the municipal instructors accepted the materials from the interviewers, and the municipal commission checked, again, the completeness of the material for the entire municipality. Thereafter, the material was provided to the central census commission for the entire republic, or Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, who again conducted some checks of completeness, especially geographic completeness of the questionnaires. Afterwards, based on basically manual counting of information from census questionnaires, some preliminary statistics were published already in 1991, two months after the census was over. These were called preliminary statistics, and by this, the central statistical authority reserved the right to revise statistics once the entire material will be in the system, electronic system, and again checked and processed. The authorities of Bosnia and Herzegovina decided to computerised this material by optical scanning, so these census questionnaires were not entered by data entry clerks but were scanned. So immediately after the material was received in the central statistical office, the authorities started preparing for optical scanning. That means questionnaires were reviewed, all the questionnaires were reviewed from the point of view where the information is coded, whenever necessary, and whether it's readable for -- from the point of view of the technicalities of the process. Optical scanning was finished, I think, in the beginning of the 1992. Then, at this stage, electronic database could be established in which the authorities could engage in certain checks. These are -- checks were called logical controls, relationships between related variables were studied. And whenever necessary, corrections were made to the census data. An example of such a relationship is, for instance, for a child of ten years old, marital status cannot be that the person is marries. So this is the type of logical controls that were conducted. There were also other checks. And the portion of information related to the population was checked completely. This cannot be said about the agricultural census and housing part of the census. So this particular census had three parts: Population, housing, and agriculture. So for populations, checks were finished; not for agriculture; and not for housing. At that stage, the work kind of stopped because of the war. The authorities never completed the checks for the two other parts of the census, but they did prepare some publications related to the population. The publications were issued already in 1995. Data was provided to the Croatian Statistical Office. And then a publication was made for settlements --

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I'll just interrupt you and ask you to slow down a bit.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And can I also ask you to give us a more summarized view of the procedure from the collection of the statistics through scanning through the raw data and its arrival to you in the OTP Demographics Unit.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if I'm going there, only that I will -- received the data in around 1998, and I'm trying to say what happened with the data in, in the meantime. And by saying that the data was published, the data on population, ethnic composition, religion, I'm trying to say that according to the authorities the data was good enough to come up with official statistics based on the 1991 census. So they obviously have done a lot of work with the data. They published some statistics. And at that point we requested to receive a copy of individual census records for our purposes. So we received an electronic version of the data, of which we, ourselves, established our databases and compiled our own statistics.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Okay. So, you went from collect -- initial collection, through various checks and -- various checks to make sure that the material was collected properly, further checks in Bosnia to make sure that it was coherent and logical, scanned, put into electronic data form, and eventually received by the Demographics Unit. Is that a basic but correct sequence of the way in which the material was dealt with?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thanks. Focus now on the point of time when the materials arrived here at the OTP Demographics Unit. You -- you discuss various problems that you had to look at, including problems with the Maticni Broj or identification number. I don't want to deal with that. One of the other problems you referred to was spelling mistakes in the data. Could you please inform the Trial Chamber of what the significance of the spelling mistakes were and how the OTP went about dealing with the problem.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Spelling mistakes in the names was, for us, a major issue. Well, it is -- I want to mention that it is not common for statistical authority to provide data to an outside user - data, individual data - with names. They did it for us at our request and with the understanding that information about names and other personal items is essential in our work. So statistical authority normally do not work with names. They do not clean up the names. They do not process the names, because that's the confidential part of information. This is the part that is removed from the data while making statistics. So we have to sort out this problem here, and we did. We -- there was several procedures we applied to correct the spelling mistakes. One can imagine there are quite many spelling mistakes after optical scanning, as that is the misreading of certain characters by even the best computer programmes. So these misshaped, misread characters must be corrected. Some must be removed altogether, some must be replaced by the right characters. First of all, we developed a computer programme code which was automatically searching for misshaped characters and impossible combinations of letters in the Serbo-Croat, in the B/C/S language. These combinations were identified and were studied by native speakers, and the native speakers made proposals about how to correct them. So once this was done, the corrections were introduced back in the names. And in the second step, frequency tables were made with the names, with the replaced characters. These actual names, both surnames and first names, were again studied by the native speakers who went and visually checked every name in these tables and corrected, whenever necessary, to make a name correct from the point of view of the language and naming traditions in Bosnia and Herzegovina. These corrected names were again introduced back in the data. So incorrect names were replaced by the corrected names. Finally, we again thought there is a need for some more work on these. He we applied a so-called household method. In the census records there is information about the household composition for every household, so we checked how the surnames are reported within households and compared the different spellings within each household. All the incorrect spellings were then replaced by the correct spelling for every household.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: But we still keep a record of both originally scanned names and corrected names. So there is a bridging system between the two, and every name can be accessed. There is quite a lot of, I think, yeah, correspondence to -- between these two.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you for that explanation. So that's how you went about cleaning up the material that you received to make sure that you had corrected names. Just explain, please, to the Trial Chamber why it was so important -- or why, for your purposes, to -- to conduct this exercise to make sure that you had correctly spelled names?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: The basic concept with which my unit has been working all these years is that we trace individuals in related sources of information, starting from the information we have about the Bosnia and Herzegovina population in the 1991 census. So the census is our basis. Starting from there, we always wanted to find individuals as those reported in the census in related sources of information. It is -- it can be seen as a bit of detective work. It is just a system in which we want to know what happened to various individuals. I mean, we want to know who died, we want to know who survive. If persons died, we want to know where they died, when they died, how they died. And we have quite a number of sources that report on, on one hand, the dead population, the missing persons population, but also about post-war survives. So names from this point of view are crucial. When searching for persons, we must use the information about persons' names and other details, like date of birth, in related sources of information. Normally, in western societies, developed countries, this wouldn't be necessary because every person has an individual number, like social security number. So if one has such a number, which is consequently reported across a number of registers, then tracing individuals is not such a big issue. It is just a matter of searching for this particular ID, person ID, in sources, in various sources. That, however, is not the case in the former Yugoslavia, even though individuals started to be assigned personal identification numbers. In the early 1980s, these numbers were only used in the 1991 census and a few other sources, but the expectation that these numbers were used in sources on war victims, missing persons, is simply wrong. Such numbers were not included there. So the other alternative was searching for persons using names. I'm using the term "searching." As a matter of fact, searching, in this context, should be seen as "matching." Matching records representing the same persons in various sources.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Hence, the need for an absolutely correct name that you know is talking -- that relates to a real individual?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Matching, of course, relates to individuals. It is, as I said, looking for the same individual in various sources of information, using names, date of birth, place of birth, other characteristics. That is the magic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you very much for that explanation. The census, of course, provided lots of information about an individual, including where they lived. One of the other bits of information that was provided was ethnicity, whether they're Muslims, Croat, or other. First of all - and please give us as brief an answer as possible - the census, did it permit a person to write the whole -- quite a large choice of answers to provide when asked about ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was an open-ended question in the census, so anybody and everybody could report whatever they felt they were, in terms of ethnic affiliations. As a outcome, final outcome, of the responses, we see a list of 98 categories, three of which are major ethnic groups who lived in Bosnia and Herzegovina, Muslims, Serbs, Croats. And the remaining categories represent either mixed categories, Serbo-Croat, for instance. Or there is an number of individuals who identified themselves as Yugoslavs. And there are nationalities like Hungarian, Polish, French, German reported under this term as well. So it was an open-ended question.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thanks. So the source of someone's ethnicity in all of your reports originates with that what person said about themselves?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And the -- the issue of ethnicity, was the information in all of your three reports, concerning ethnicity, did it only ever come from the census information; or did you use any other statistics or other source?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, obviously ethnicity is our major concern, analytical concern, I mean, because we want to know how the ethnic composition of the population changed, what was the ethnic make-up of the victims. These are basic questions that we have to answer in our work. So ethnicity if extremely important. Ethnicity, ideally, shouldn't be used based on the reporting from various sources. This is because people tend to change their perceptions of ethnicity. And it a well-known fact that political economic social situation has a huge impact on how the people see themselves in concrete socio-economic context. So the elimination of any bias, analytical bias, related to ethnicity, was our major concern, of course. For this reason, we decided to use, in any report that we will make, only one definition of ethnicity. This was the definition taken from the 1991 population census. Moreover, we decided not to work with 98 categories, as reported, because it's far too many for any analytical report, so we decided to group the ethnicities other than the three major ethnic groups. So we separated Muslims, Serbs, and Croats as the major ethnic groups, major from the point of view of our interest. And the remaining ethnicities, whatever answer would it be, Yugoslav, mixed ethnicities, nationalities, were grouped together under one category, the so-called others. As a matter of fact, we had four mainly ethnic groups in our analysis. And thanks to the fact that related sources of information, be them dead, missing persons, or postwar survivors, these sources, thanks to the matching with the census records, could be shown in our analysis according to the ethnicity reported in the 1991 census. What I said now is quite a complex issue. I'm speaking of transferring information from the 1991 census through the matches, through the links established between the records. So ethnicity from the census is transferred through the links between the records into the related sources of information.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Okay. But in very simple terms, and trying and keep it as simple as possible, whether someone, for the purposes of your statistical sources, is -- is a Muslim or a Serb depends on what they said in the 1991 census. You didn't go to any other source taken during the war or after the war asking the same question: What are you, a Muslim or a Serb? Do you understand my point?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do understand your point. Of course, that is my point too. So we never used any other ethnicity [sic] than the one from the 1991 census.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Let's turn briefly to the OSCE voters' register. You -- I'm not going to into the way in which you dealt with the material there, but I just want you to basically explain what it was to the Trial Chamber. Obviously it's voters who registered to vote in Bosnia. And when did they register?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: The voters' register of 1997 was established for the September 1997 municipal elections in Bosnia and Herzegovina by the OSCE, together with local authorities. And the one for 1998 election, it was register largely based on the one for the 1997 election, but meant for an election that -- parliamentary election that took place one year later. The registration of the eligible voters took place around May/June, as far as I remember, of 1997. And for 1998 election, accordingly, one year later. So as a matter of fact, the voters' register is a huge list of all individuals in Bosnia and Herzegovina who were eligible to vote in 1997 and 1998 elections. Eligible to vote relates to -- the term "eligible to vote" relates to the age, of course. One has to be at least 18 in order to be eligible. But there was another important requirement: To be eligible to vote in these particular elections, first -- one of the first democratic elections in the country, it was necessary to be listed in the population census of 1991 as the citizen of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. And I think your -- the expression you're using is "eligible," not "legible."

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Eligible, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: All right. So you've got these two sets of numbers from -- sorry, statistical sources from 1997 and 1998. Did you compare them and see if they overlapped?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: They overlapped greatly. As a matter of fact, the 1998 list of eligible voters is -- only contains approximately 150.000 new registrations in 1998 and the rest were voters already registered for the 1997 elections.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: So that means that the majority of the -- the greater part of this statistical source consists of people who registered in 1997?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is correct. Well, we actually, as a matter of fact, merged, or combined, in other words, the two registers into one, and we did in such a way that we took first registrations from 1997 as the core of this merged register, and from the 1998 register, it is only the new registrations. So as a matter of fact, I often even say it is voters' register 1997 because it represents the situation as of this period of time. Not exclusively, but greatly. This is the majority of information in this register that is associated with the 1997 -- year of 1997.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And the effect of that is -- let me rephrase my question. Your -- the Milosevic report and the addendum report prepared specifically for this case very basically compares the -- the 1991 census and these voters' registers in order to examine population movement by way of ethnicity. The fact that there was a large overlap means that the time-frame between the two snap-shot pictures that you are looking at is reduced. It's 1991 and mostly 1997, not 1998. Do you understand my question?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We, indeed, in our Milosevic report and the addendum based on the Milosevic report made for this case, we did, indeed, looked at the situation in 1991, based on the census, and in 1997, based on the integrated merged voters' register, 1997, 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like to take you to your major conclusions for the Stanisic/Zupljanin addendum report.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Can we have 65 ter 10397 on the screen, please. Can we focus a bit more on the set of numbers at the top the page. Table 1 basically. Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I'd like you to explain -- sorry. Let me start again. This is the summary that you prepared of the principle findings from the Stanisic/Zupljanin IDP report; correct?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Okay. Let's took at Table 1 on that. The first row -- sorry. My apologies. The first column, that's -- they're the figures for the Stanisic/Zupljanin indictment area for -- obtained from the 1991 census; is that right?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the first column, indeed, we have some statistics based on census data. They covered, indeed, the Stanisic/Zupljanin case study area. That means, in this case, 18 municipalities specified in the report. Importantly, these statistics, it is the population size, basically, in this column, by ethnicity, only covers the individuals that were eligible to vote in 1997/1998 elections. It is a sample -- well, it is not a sample. It is a subpopulation reported in the census of the individuals born before 1980. And we took this subpopulation in order to be able to match these individuals with the voters registered for the 1997/1998 elections, and based on the matches that we would be able to compare these individuals from the point of ethnicity, the ethnic composition, and from the point of view of their place of residence in 1991 and 1997, 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Okay. So these 817.898 people that we see there have two qualities: First of all, they were mentioned in the 1991 census; and secondly they were eligible to vote in 1997, 1998?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And they all come from the Stanisic/Zupljanin case study area?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Okay. Could we please go to the second column, the minimum number. What is that a minimum number of?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is the minimum number of internally displaced person and refugees, as the title of this table says, that we obtained based on our methodology and our sources.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And these are actual individuals, actual numbers of -- yes, of individuals?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are numbers of individuals that we identified, that they changed their place of residence in 1997/1998, as compared where they lived at the outbreak of the war in 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: So for the Stanisic/Zupljanin case study area, 40.895 Serbs, at least, were displaced?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is correct. This is the term we use in our report to describe these individuals. And it is perhaps important to mention that the term "displaced" statistically means that the person have totally different residence, place of residence, in 1997/1998 compared with 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. And for Muslims, that figure of -- is 119.000-odd?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is approximately 119.000 and is the largest number among all ethnicities.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Now, they -- we can see what -- the numbers there, and we can see what they are applying to, Croats and others. By far the biggest figure there is Muslims. The next column that you have is the estimated number. Now, is that an extrapolation that the OTP Demographics Unit arrived at?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is an extrapolation. While the minimum number can be documented by personal details of all persons reported as displaced or refugees, the estimated number is composed of the minimum number plus, on the top of it, an extra part that comes from our extrapolation procedure, statistical estimation procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: So you applied your expertise as a demographer, and you estimated that the real number is, in fact, higher than those of -- indicated by the minimum numbers.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The minimum number is obviously incomplete for several reason; one reason being that not all voters eligible to vote registered and participated in the elections. There are other reasons as well, like, for instance, that our matching rate was not 100 per cent, was lower than 100 per cent, meaning that -- as a matter of fact, it was approximately 80 per cent that -- meaning that 80 per cent of the voters' records were matched with the census records. So that is the 20 per cent records that remain unmatched, and these unmatched records cannot be taken for the analysis because we don't have information about ethnicity, we don't have information about their place of residence back in 1991. So these are the main reasons that this number is incomplete. To compensate for this incompleteness, there is a need to apply a statistical estimation technique which give us a more complete number. This is a simple technique, a standard statistical method that is used for ages in statistics. It is a method based on extrapolation of a sample proportion, sample proportion, of displaced persons in the voters' register over the entire 1991 census population. Conceptually, the method is simple; practically, applying the formulas to our data is also simple. As a result, the outcome is a more complete number of displaced persons and refugees. As we see in the Table 1 when we compare the two, so for the Serbs we have the minimum number of approximately 41.000 individuals, and if we go to the estimated number, the estimated number is approximately 71.000 individuals. And a similar situation for every other ethnic group: For the Muslims, on one hand, the minimum number is 119.000, approximately, and the estimated number is 212.000, approximately. So for the estimated number, we also provide confidence intervals which are reported in the same table in the two columns next to the estimated number --

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Just very briefly before we move on to the confidence interval, in a nutshell, tell me if you agree with this: The minimum number relates to real numbers that you obtain from your comparisons with the 1997/1998 voters' register and the census. Using those numbers, you then extrapolated and came up the estimated number. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's in big lines. Well, minimum number is basically an empirical count. It's a count. It's a count that we obtained from counting records that we identified as displaced or refugees. Estimated number is an estimated count. That means it's a statistical product, product which is obtained from sample statistics that are extrapolated over the entire population. So in statistics, this is a regular procedure to have sample surveys, usually these are small surveys, calculate certain statistics for the samples, and applying these statistics, in terms of extrapolation, over the entire populations. This is what we have done. So the result is a number plus the confidence interval which gives us some idea about uncertainty of this estimated number.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you just explain again, please, the confidence interval?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I already mentioned, confidence intervals are meant in statistics to express the uncertainty associated with point estimates. Point estimate is just one single number. As a matter of fact, we produce our point estimates based on a given sample, but, if more samples would, say, have been taken from the same population, like ten different samples, 100 different samples, and each time the same parameter would be estimated, based on all these samples, then the results would be slightly different. So there would be a whole distribution of results, but our number from our sample we can show with a certain degree of certainty will fall under an interval, and I present here 95 per cent confidence intervals. That means with a confidence of 95 per cent, leaving the 5 per cent room for error, so with the confidence of 95 per cent, our point estimate is in this interval. So even if the other samples would have been drawn, then every next estimate would be falling -- would be contained in this interval.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Somewhere between those two numbers?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It's important to stress that narrow confidence intervals express low uncertainty, which is the case in our statistics here. That is a simple fact related to the size of our sample. The voters' register with which we work is, as a matter of fact, an enormously big sample. In statistics, often we do analysis with 2.000 respondents representing whole populations, we are speaking of 2.7 million individuals that were included in the voter's register. That is our sample of the voters' population that was approximately 3.2 million eligible voters. So we are speaking of a huge, huge, enormous sample that is used for our analysis. So it not surprising that the confidence intervals are, as a matter of fact, extremely narrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. I think that explains it. Okay. Moving down from there, just take a look at Table 2, please. That's just more of a visual representation of the numbers that we can see above; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in the table above, we have the numbers of displaced persons and refugees, but the second table actually is telling us a slightly different thing. It is the ethnic make-up --

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- ethnic composition of the population as it was in 1995 -- 1991 and as it changed in 1997.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. Okay. Yes, my mistake, and I'm grateful to you for correcting me. So the -- in the case study area for the Stanisic/Zupljanin study, you can see the number of Serbs represented by this bar chart. Obviously its increased considerably and the Muslims have decreased considerably between 1991 and 1997. That's the significance of those -- of that picture.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is correct. And I would like to mention one important observation. The 1997 population is a sample, so please don't take absolute numbers as the actual representation of the 1997 population. These are minimum numbers. But if you look at percentages, the ethnic make-up, the ethnic composition expressed in percentages in the second panel of this table, so the percentages can be compared between 1991 and 1997. This is what I'm saying. So I'm saying please do not compare absolute numbers. Please do not look at 1991 population that used to be 818.000, approximately, in 1991 and in 1997 is reported as 376.000, approximately - that would be a large drop in the absolute size - please don't do that because that is not really correct. But do -- the sample of voters is a sample. It is not the entire population of voters, right, unlike the 1991 population, which is complete population, as reported in the census. However, if we go to percentages, if we go to percentages, these percentages can be directly compared between the two years, in 1991 and 1997. So if we look at the Muslims' population, we see, for 1991, the number of 35.2 per cent reported. There were 35.2 per cent Muslims in 1991, in the study area of Stanisic/Zupljanin case; however, in 1997, there are only 18.4 per cent Muslims remaining in this area.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And conversely, for the Serbs --

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: And conversely for the Serbs, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... 1991, 44 per cent in the case study area. In 1997, that figure had gone to 72 per cent.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: So that is what is shown on the figure, the percentages, the percentages. These are directly comparable. So the drop in Muslim the population and the increase in the Serb population, that is what we really can take as a fact, as a fact. There was a significant drop in the non-Serb population, not only of Muslims but also Croats and others, and there was a significant increase in the Serb population in this area by 1997, when compared with 1991.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Di Fazio, if you allow, Ms. Tabeau, just for my understanding, the numbers in the first part of Table 2, if I understand it correctly, 1991, that's a count of the effective population?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: That's a total count?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: But 1997 is not a total count?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is also correct. This is only those voters who registered to vote.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Only the voters who registered --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... registered to vote. So those unregistered and unmatched are not there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So that is why it is a sample -- [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: So we don't know -- we don't know whether the, if I take the figures, all inhabitants, 1991 and 1997, we don't know, if I may so, what happened to the - what is it? - 400.000 that are not in the sample or how they are ethnically composed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, basically, I would disagree with that because based on the analysis of the large sample of the registered voters, we do know what happened to the entire population. We are unable to give absolute numbers, complete numbers, because the size of the population in terms of absolute numbers, 1997/1998, is unknown until today. The size of the actual --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... I do -- I do agree.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: So you don't have the actual numbers of the total population --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: -- and you had to do with that sample.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: But is that sample not influenced, or did you examine whether that sample is influenced, I mean, on the ethnic composition of it by a wilful act of the people who wanted to register as voters and the wilful act of those who didn't want to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The participation rate in the 1997 election was extremely high. It was higher than 80 per cent. So this is -- the assessment --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Higher than 80 per cent of what?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Participation rate. Participation rate. This is the assessment of the OSCE. That means a large group of eligible voters registered to vote. The large group registered to vote. So that means it is such a large representation that entire population that, statistically speaking, it is most certainly a representative representation of the entire population. So that we miss -- yes?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: But 80 per cent of what exactly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of the eligible voters registered to vote and participated in the election. This is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So it is, as a matter of fact, a very large representation. So we don't have -- when we speak of the voters' register as a sample, I think the discussion of any bias related to non-registered voters I think is, statistically speaking, not really relevant, because 80 per cent registered, and for them we have very specific information about where they registered, where they lived. I think that is all I can say. It is -- for 1991, we have the complete record of the population. For 1997/1998, we have a large sample, a large sample that is representative of the actual population. Well, as a matter of fact, it will be very hard to even explore those unregistered voters because there is no record of them other than they are in the census. So we do have information from the census, right? But we don't know how they moved, whether they became displaced or not in 1997/1998. So from this point of view there is nothing that can be done, as a matter of fact. I -- I have no doubt whatsoever that the ethnic composition and our estimation of the ethnic composition is very good and unbiased because of the statistical properties of this sample.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I think this is a convenient point to take the break. We return in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Before the -- we resume with the witness, there's a matter that's unresolved from yesterday. The OTP had requested, or indicated that it would request, an extended sitting tomorrow in order to complete one of the witnesses scheduled for this week, and we hadn't gotten a -- we said we would inquire of the Defence this morning as to what their reaction was to that -- to that proposal. First of all, in terms of the remainder of this week, is it still the OTP's view that an extended sitting is necessary? And before you answer, I would remind you that it is only one session that is possibly available and that is tomorrow afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think it's still our position that we think it will be necessary to have that extra one session in order to -- to complete the next witness and the additional two crime-based witnesses that we've scheduled for this week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Sorry. Today is Wednesday. We have a witness who has just started her testimony. You said the next witness and then two other witnesses?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, ST-163.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: But not 227 and 251.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Our primary concern is to be able to finish Witness ST-163 this week. The other two witnesses that were previously scheduled for this week are crime-based witnesses addressing adjudicated facts, and they should be fairly short. And if we have time on Friday to do one or both of them, we hope to do that. But, if not, we'll push them off to next week or some later date. But our primary concern was to have that extra session in order to be sure that we completed ST-163.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: And I take it that the Defence, having had overnight to consider it, has no difficulty with the one extra session tomorrow afternoon?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, there will be no problem with one session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic, your position is likewise?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we don't have a problem with that extra session. But as far as I understood the OTP position, I think it is their problem, because when I spoke to the witness, I heard he to travel on Friday morning. I'm talking about ST-163. He has to travel to attend a family event on Saturday. So I don't think one session will help, if he has to complete his testimony tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Well, the reality is that there's only one session available. So if there is no problem with it, we will plan accordingly. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: The session would -- thank you. The session would be from 2.30 to 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Di Fazio, just one follow-up question for the witness, please. Madam Tabeau, the 80 per cent we were talking about, the 80 per cent of registered voters. How is that 80 per cent determined?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is an assessment made by OSCE who were monitoring the elections, who were present in every office where the voters registered and, well, I believe were in touch with local authorities. I said there is no record of the population size as of this time, 1997/1998.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: And there is no -- there is no register of possible eligible voters? So it's an estimation. The 80 per cent is an estimation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There is no register other than population census. As I said, to be eligible, one had to be reported in the population census. And the age was required 18 years, right. But I can imagine, and this is my theory, that the local authorities did have information about the local populations living in the municipalities. I guess that based on the census, on one hand, the record of population eligible to vote in the census plus the information of the local populations, OSCE was able to produce this estimate. I don't know the technicalities, I don't know the method, but it is quite normal that the international monitors, OSCE, present this kind of rates, participation rates. And as a matter of fact, I said it was 80 per cent. I saw two alternative estimates. In one report, OSCE report, I said I saw 80 per cent participation rate, and in another I saw 89 participation rate. I took the lower to be conservative, and not to overestimate. However, it is at least 80 per cent. And judging, in addition, from the size of the register itself, for 1997 it was 2.6 million individuals registered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So if you apply the 80 per cent, you end with the required size of all eligible to vote. So that is a straightforward calculation. So statistically, it is at least 80 per cent who registered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Part of your Stanisic/Zupljanin case-specific report refers to some limited aggregate statistics based on documentation obtained from the Republika Srpska authorities. And I think you provide an overview of that at Annex A5 as well. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I just want to show you two of the document -- two documents, and can you tell us if these are the documents that you used and that were obtained from the Republika Srpska authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Can we have P425, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Is that the document that you used?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, of course. But the 12 databases you have just mentioned are, as a matter of fact, 12 large sources that report on deaths or missing persons. These are sources on victims. And this is war victims. These sources are broader than the study case area, Stanisic/Zupljanin study case area. They cover, as a matter of fact, the entire territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina and entire war period. Having said this, for this particular report, for this case, I only used a part, a portion, of all these 12 databases. Portion that is relevant to this study area, indictment area, and indictment period. And in addition to this, I also used, among others, the population census of 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thanks. The -- from these -- from the information that you obtained -- you obtained from the 12 databases, you, I believe, were able to get a list of people killed in that time-period and in that area, eventually, after conducting all your studies; right?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: As a matter of fact, it is the list of people killed and -- or who went missing, who disappeared, and are reported as missing persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: How did you make sure that they hadn't -- that people who were listed as killed in the -- in this list of statistical sources, the 12 databases were, in fact, killed and didn't turn up and vote, for example, in 1997?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we -- as I said, I used the census, the 12 sources on victims. But also other sources that you were used. The voters' records were used in order to eliminate false positives. That means if -- dead people cannot be alive at the same time. So if there is an alive person, this person has to go. But this is a complex issue. As a matter of fact, as -- while there is, as a matter of fact, little interest of the living population in reporting false positive as dead people, then records of dead people can be sometimes found in the voters' register. So as a matter of fact, what I'm trying to say is it's not a straightforward issue to decide, even if there is a match between a record of a dead person or missing persons with the voter record, that this person has not died or -- and survived the war. This is what I'm trying to say. I'm not -- so, yeah. I -- I will use an example. In Srebrenica cases, we studied -- we identified 24, approximately, 24 records in the voters' register of Srebrenica victims. We studied these records and compared how they were reported in the voters' register 1997, 1998, and another source on surviving population. We have a registration of internally displaced person and refugees. And these 24 records were reported in some of these sources and a few of them in all three sources. At the same time, these persons were all reported as missing persons from Srebrenica. And for some of these persons, we had DNA identification reports based on the DNA study of the remains from exhumations. So obviously they cannot be both dead and surviving. The problem is -- well, we studied these records. We distinguished the records reported in all three sources on surviving population and distinguished the records for whom that DNA identification was possible. So for these records for whom the DNA identification is obtained, obviously, are confirmed dead. There is a proof of death. This is a DNA matching result with the surviving family members. So in this situation, we accepted the superiority of this reporting. And from the 24 initially reported as potential survivors, we accepted 12 as possible survivors and rejected 12 as confirmed deaths. So this -- what I'm trying to say, these are complex issues. There are examples of families who reported dead people as IDPs in order to obtain more aid. These are practicalities of life in a war-affected country. So we did our best and flagged all records of dead people in the voters' register. And these records shouldn't be reported among the dead or missing persons. However, as a matter of fact, it is in my view an extremely conservative approach which eliminates --

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] ... slow down a bit, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- which eliminates a number of actual deaths. That is what I'm saying. But we, nevertheless, did control for the reporting of records in the voters' register. That was part of our methodology. We've been using this methodology for a long time. Well, we call this methodology a proof-of-death methodology. In brief, this methodology is: Once we have a list of victims - it can be a list from the indictment schedules - we look at this list, we check how these victims are reported in our 12 sources on war victims, on one hand, we link these records with the 1991 census to confirm the personal details and the -- the actual fact that these are people from Bosnia and Herzegovina. We do look at voters' register and make a summary of all these results. So that is what we usually do to provide as much information as possible on every victim.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thanks. As brief as possible, can you tell the Trial Chamber if you found anything significant or any significant numbers of people that you had isolated from the 12 databases as being people killed during the indictment period and in the indictment area and later turned up as having registered to vote.

So, as a matter of fact, these kind of marginal numbers do not have any significant impact on the overall picture that is presented in our victims report.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you.
