But you reject -- you included some and you rejected others. What -- what features did the ones you accepted have, and what features did the ones you rejected have, in order to come up with your final list of numbers?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 12 sources, or databases as you say, are the essential part of our method. This is not that we use just any source on victims of war. These are 12 sources that we consider the best existing sources on war victims for Bosnia and Herzegovina. Among them we have exhumation records; among them we have DNA identification records; we have missing persons records of ICMP; we have records from military lists, that is, the military records of fallen soldiers and associated military personnel; we have, finally, records from official death notifications from both authorities of the FBiH and RS statistical authority, who compiled a wartime registration of these deaths at our request and provided this for use in my unit in the ICTY cases. So, sources that we have selected for this report and several other reports are not accidental. They are large, they are relatively less, far less, deficient than any other source, yet they are not complete. But going to the point. Some sources that he we have at our disposal were not used in this work. And I'm giving examples of these sources in my report. These were sources compiled by all sides, by Bosniaks, by Serbs, and also by Croats. And the main reason is that, first of all, the coverage of the rejected sources is already very good in the sources included among the 12; that is one thing. And the quality of reporting in the rejected sources is far lower than the quality of reporting than in the included sources. Reliability is another issue. The sources we included have been inspected, as also the other sources. And we believe the reliability of these sources is generally good. So these are the reasons for rejections.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thanks for explaining that. And one last question about the databases. You've mentioned 12 databases. Did you do anything to check to make sure that people weren't being counted more than once? In other words, that you, you know, you got rid of duplicates within a database, as opposed to, with any one database, the 11 others?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We, of course, always check for duplicates, first within each source. And then when we combine sources, when we match sources, integrate sources, we look at the overlap. That would be the duplicate between the sources. Of course, duplicates and overlap have to go, so what remains are records representing different individuals.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And that final set of numbers or -- that final statistical source is what you refer to as the "integrated database" in your report; am I right?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is correct. This integrated mortality database, as we call it, is a database for Bosnia and Herzegovina, the entire country, as we didn't do it only for this case, we did it for the entire country in order to be able to extract statistics for any case, any episode of the war, any incident even. So this is the integrated mortality database. Its coverage is Bosnia and Herzegovina and the entire war period. From this database, relevant records were extracted for this report, Stanisic/Zupljanin victims report, on the basis on the two criteria: Territory, that would be the indictment municipalities, and the time-frame, that would be the period of the indictment, April to December 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Can we please get page 8 of the "Victims of War" report - that's 65 ter 10400 - up on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: There's just one table that I want you to look at in particular from your report.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: So it's page 8 of the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Okay. You also have it in front of you in hard copy, I believe. I want to get through this swiftly, if we can, please, Madam Tabeau. Table 1. Is the figures that you see there are figures that you obtained from these 12 databases, and are they Bosnia-wide, that is, not just confined to the indictment area?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. And you can see we've only got 8 databases there. And so far we've been speaking about 12. What's the explanation for that?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 12 sources have been grouped for radical purposes for a report that we present later. And there have been made eight groups out of the 12 sources. Sources of similar nature are combined together. Like, for instance, FIS, RS, and most are death notifications. They all represent the same type of sources. It is, therefore, one group, numbered 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's go to the first column. The source size overlap contained. What do those numbers that you can see there represent?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is the size of the sources, source by source. So the overall total of 181.000, approximately, is the overall total of initial records taken for the analysis.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thanks. Moving on to the next column. The source size overlap, overlap excluded. What does that represent?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: That means overlap is not there. So what remain is the records, unique records representing different persons. For Bosnia and Herzegovina, such a number is 89.881, which is almost 90.000 records for the entire war period.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Okay. So the "overlap excluded" means you got rid of the duplicates and so on and these are the final figures, not including any duplicates?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Okay. So 89.881 dead in Bosnia for that time-period, 1992 to 1995?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is the minimum number again, as unusual inn our analyses.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank. 89.881 dead soldiers and civilians?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dead and missing; right? Dead and missing persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And amongst the dead, that includes soldiers and civilians?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Just explain the next column, please, matching rates with the 1991 census. What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the percentage of records, source by source, that have been matched with the population census. All together, for -- as an average, there is 89.5 per cent reported. That is almost 90 per cent, which is -- which is very high rate. Usually it is very hard to obtain this kind of matching.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... thanks --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Di Fazio, just one moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Ms. Tabeau, does that mean that more or less 10 per cent of the records, that people in those records were not in the 1991 census and probably came from elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it doesn't mean that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: No. Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That only means we were unable to declare this remaining 10 per cent as matched. And this was caused by --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- deficiencies in reporting. An example --

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... you couldn't find them in -- you couldn't find them --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We couldn't find them in the census. We couldn't find them in the census because of the deficiencies in reporting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, that's all I want on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Di Fazio, may I remind you that you have about five minutes left of your time, so you should round up.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have done better than I thought. Would you be minded to give me an extra ten or 15 minutes? It's -- I can tell you what issues I want to cover. I want to cover the final summary of this report, which I think is clearly the most important remaining topic. But there's just one or two other issues that I want to very briefly cover and that is the -- the issue of the division of numbers into war-related deaths -- sorry, to civilian deaths and military deaths. That might just take me over.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: You have until the break, Mr. Di Fazio. That's a total of 15 -- of 16 minutes. Sorry, yeah, 16 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: All right. Thank you, Your Honours. Can we go to 65 ter 10400.2, please. And get that up on the screen, if we may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Di Fazio, we're advised that this number is not in the system.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: 10400.2. Would Your Honours just give me a moment. Sorry, it's .02, apparently. Is that number -- that's it, that's the one. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: This is your -- what it says, it is main findings. Now, this relates to the main findings derived from the numbers of people killed in the indictment area in this case and also during the period of time, April to December 1992. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Okay. Again, the minimum number that we see there at the top, 12.000 people killed in the indictment area and for that period of time, that's just the -- that minimum number is -- is individual records, based on individual persons; right?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. These are individual records that are documented in our 12 sources. And for them we can give personal details as well as details of their death or disappearance in terms of time and area. And several other items can be provided as well for every victim.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Okay. Now, we see there an estimated overall number, and we can tell from the components of the overall total that that estimated overall number is made up of the minimum number which we know about, plus something called exclusions and the estimated undercount. Now I want you, just very briefly -- very briefly and succinctly tell the Trial Chamber what exclusions are. And then when you've done that, what the estimated undercount is. Again, being as brief as you can.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. First of all, we have a minimum number. It is called minimum because our sources are incomplete. There is a part which is missing, and we don't know what part is missing. This can be statistically estimated using certain modern techniques. And this is, in our report, in our work, called estimation of the undercount of the undercount, that is, of what is not counted. However, when we extracted records, as I said, we used two criteria: Time and area. There is a number of records reported in the database incompletely. We know they are deaths or missing persons from 1992, but we don't know exactly what month in 1992. So such records had to be excluded from our minimum number. Or we know these records were in the time-frame of this indictment but we didn't know the municipality of that, so these records had to be excluded. So the minimum number is minimal in two ways. First of all, because in our records not all relevant records could be taken, and, secondly, because sources are incomplete. So the first component, 2.278 is our statistical estimate of the records that could not be taken from our databases because of the missing data items. And the second component is the undercount estimate, that is, the part of the information that is completely uncovered by our sources. And the methodology of obtaining both these numbers is explained in the annex to our report with details. All together, these two undercount estimates amount to approximately 5.000 cases that are not included in our minimum number. So the estimated number, overall estimated number, is not 12.047 but 17.060 killed and missing persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Okay. Thanks for that explanation. Then you talk about the division into military and civilian victims. Is that -- 37.8 and 62 per cent civilians, is that based on the estimated overall number or the minimum number?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is based on the minimum number, that is, on the numbers -- of the number of 12.000, approximately. So these are the documented victims. And the distribution into military and civilian comes as part of our methodology. Is based on the reporting in our sources.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. And then you -- finally, you give this ethnic distribution of civilians. Now, of the civilians from this number of 17 -- sorry, 12.047, of the civilians, taking away the soldiers and military, 84 per cent of them were Muslim; is that a correct statement of that -- how that figure's derived?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The -- approximately 85 per cent of civilian victims were of Muslim ethnicity. About 8 per cent were Serbs; three and a half, Croats; 3.8, others. That is the civilian victims, the ethnic composition of the civilian victims.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... civilian -- civilian victims.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now, it is -- the civilian victims as we see in Table 3 towards the end of the same page, towards the end of the same page. So it's page -- first 1 -- page 1. So in the first column of Table 3, we have an absolute number of civilians and militaries. The number of civilians is 7.499. 704.099. [Sic] This is the minimum number of civilians. And of them, approximately 85 per cent were Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thanks.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is what we are talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. In the -- quickly go through figure 4. Firstly, that -- I don't know what you call it, a bar table, or that type of representation?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Bar chart.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Bar chart, thank you. Bar chart. That's based on the minimum number, 12.047, not 17.000.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's correct. It's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Okay. And let's just take a moment to look at that. Of all Muslims who were killed, individuals here, we've got individuals, not -- not based on extrapolations or statistical methods but just the minimum number, of all Muslims who were killed in April to December of 1992, and who lived in the Stanisic/Zupljanin area, indictment area, about 65 per cent of them were civilians.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Strictly, speaking, it is exactly two thirds, that is, 66.7 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... yeah --

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Two thirds of Muslims --

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... right --

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- were civilians, and one third is reported as militaries in our sources.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And the other feature that immediately jumps out at you from that bar chart is that of Croats and the others, the group called "others," it was civilians who were disproportionately killed, as opposed to military, but quite the opposite for Serbs. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the Serbs, for the Serb victims, the proportions are opposite. 34 per cent were civilians and 66 per cent were soldiers. So for the non-Serbs, we observed the distribution two-thirds civilians, one-third militaries; and for the Serbs, the other way around, generally speaking.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Can we have the next page please, page 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I want you to look at Figure 5. Now, you see 1992 and the following -- and this bar chart deals with 1992, 1993, 1994, and 1995.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Okay. Does it deal with the Stanisic/Zupljanin indictment area?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It contains statistics only related to the 20 municipalities from the indictment.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. So it relates to our indictment area but not our indictment period, because obviously it goes into the following years.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Okay. And you obtained these figures from your Bosnia-wide study?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Okay. So we can see that for Muslims in the indictment area, 1992 was a dramatic year by far. The vast majority of them were killed in that year.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And, well, it's -- it's obvious what -- what -- the remainder of 1993 and 1994 were, if I can put it this way, relatively quiet years in terms of deaths. And the again in 1995 there was a spike again; right?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And those figures include both soldiers and civilians.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: All lumped together.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: In -- go to Figure 7. Now, this, on the other hand, focuses on the months of 1992. And I suppose you got time of death from the 12 databases, that they had the period of time when the person died, obviously?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yeah. Okay. And, again, focus on the green for the -- representing Muslims. We can see that in 1992, and I'm looking at the first Figure 7 which only relates to civilians; right?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Right. In 1992, for civilians living in the Stanisic/Zupljanin area, from April to December of that year, by far, the worse months for them were May, June, and July, when, obviously, the majority of them were killed.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Okay. And we can see the same again at the bottom for militaries. And my last question is just this: The -- is there any significance in the scale? I look at the scale of civilians. At the top there, there's 2.500 - and I'm looking at Figure 7 - and for militaries, it's 1.600.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's correct. So the scale is broader for civilians, being that larger numbers generally were killed in at least these three top months. But another observation is that this pattern shown for civilians and soldiers is not identical. For soldiers, there is one month, June, which represents a peak of deaths, unlike for the civilians. Simply speaking, it is not only the scale so that the numbers of civilians were greater than soldiers but also that the pattern is not the same, so there is no direct association or one-to-one correspondence between the two.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes, yes. So from -- over May -- over three months, May, June, and July, a lot more civilians were being killed than for soldiers who were mainly killed, or were significantly killed, higher numbers killed in June; right?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And if Your Honours please, that brings me to the end of my examination-in-chief. Just one matter. I know, and you mentioned it, referred to it earlier, you wanted to -- you'll make a decision on which parts of the Milosevic report will go in. You want to make that decision having heard all the evidence of this witness. May I just say this to you, that for the purposes of understanding all of this evidence and -- yes. The parts that the Prosecution submit to you ought to include, you ought to include, if you're minded to make the order, is this: Section 1, objective and scope from the Milosevic report; Annex B, overview of sources, in its entirety; Annex C, overview of methods of the analysis; and, of course, the Annex D, professional qualifications of the authors. They are the most significant parts of the Milosevic report that the Prosecution says you really need in order to understand the IDP reports. And, of course, I'll be -- when you eventually make your orders, I'll be asking that the corrections and the summaries go in as part of the full list of exhibits from this body of evidence. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. So we take the break now and resume in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: If Your Honours please, perhaps before the witness continues, one particular document I didn't use with the witness - I don't think it's necessary to, I hope - it was an addendum to her "Victims of War" report, correcting some typos and some tables. It was prepared before the summer break. It wasn't necessary for my purposes to go through it this morning. It's 65 ter 10400.01. If there's no objection by the Defence, then I would ask that you eventually consider that for inclusion when you come to make your orders regarding the expert reports. It's just, as I said, an addendum, some corrections in relation to the "Victims of War" report. And, of course, if you admit that, then this should be part of it. I don't need to go into it in any more detail than that. So 65 ter 10400.01.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Aleksic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, ma'am. My name is Aleksandar Aleksic. I'm a member of the Defence team of Mr. Stojan Zupljanin, and I have a few questions for you. To avoid being repetitive, we'll sum up your examination by the OTP. As far as sources are concerned, on one hand, you had a census from 1991, and as a result of a shortage of data not generally speaking but you missed certain data from 1997, so you matched electoral data from 1997 with the 1991 census. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Would you be able to tell me, to the best of your professional knowledge, are electoral lists used anywhere else in the world for developing scientifically based reports?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Electoral lists were used for Cambodia in the estimation of the number of victims of the Khmer Rouge region in the second half of the 1970s. They were used by an American scientist, Patrick Heuveline.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: In this regard, may I ask you if that report is perhaps used in the ad hoc Tribunal for Cambodia?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: As a matter of fact, it might be. As a matter of fact, it might be. The results of his study were published in "Demography," which is the leading journal of demographers in the world. It is located in the United States of America. And Patrick Heuveline, actually his study was part of a broader overview I actually made of the victims of the Khmer Rouge regime in Cambodia. And his results were one of the more reliable, say, compared to many others by other authors. Yes. So it might be. It might be.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: As you told us at the beginning, you testified before this Tribunal in many cases and you provided numerous reports in your field.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Among other case, you testified in the Simic et al. case concerning Bosanski Samac; correct?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Let me just remind you of a certain portion of the Samac transcript dated 10 July 2002, transcript page 10784, the very end of the page, and page 10785. On page 10784, the same Prosecutor, Mr. Di Fazio, asked you to tell him something about the reliability of the sources you used for preparing your report. Going over to the next page, 10785, you answer that question, and you explain about the 1991 census, how reliable it is. And then at point 1020, you say: "Voters' register is not a source that we can consider official, not at least a source that can be used for producing official statistics. In no countries statistical authorities use these type of sources for producing statistics." I said in no, not now, "in no country." [Interpretation] Do you recall saying that in the Simic case?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I might have said it, but you, of course, skipped the context. The voters' registers are not used in -- for producing official statistics. In normal times, it is not a source that statistical authority uses to produce official statistics because there are other sources. However, in the wartime, the normal statistical sources usually. Or if exist, are incomplete and deficient. So in normal times, missing person lists are not used to calculate statistics on deaths. In normal times, exhumation records are not used to calculate statistics of killed people. But that's the difference. In normal times, we have many regular sources, especially in developed countries. And Yugoslavia -- if -- is -- if it was not most developed, it belonged to developed countries. So in normal times, we would not have to use it. But for calculating statistics related to demographic consequences of war, there is sometimes a need to use an unconventional source like the voters' register.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Very well. In your report for this case and in the course of examination-in-chief, you said that the expert report for this case is an addendum to your Milosevic report and exactly the same methods and sources were used for both; correct?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Now, in the Milosevic report, page 7 in B/C/S, paragraph 2, and page 6 in English, penultimate paragraph, you say: "One has to bear in mind that the list of voters may not be used to estimate the total population in 1997 or 1998. At that time, it was certainly over 2.7 million voters entered in the lists. However, it can be used with certainty to develop statistics, characterising ethnic make-up, and internally displaced persons and refugees in the period 1997/1998." Do you agree with this?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I recall something like that, and we already have discussed this today, as you recall, earlier today during in-chief examination. And can I only repeat what I said earlier today, that we cannot take the voters' population, that is, the voter population, as the record, complete record, of the population living in the country as of the time of the elections. But it is a large and reliable sample of this population.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: In your evidence today as well, you said that you used the lowest possible numbers, the minimum numbers from these sources, if I understood you correctly?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Now, perhaps you will not agree with me, but if these are the minimum numbers for 1997/1998, did you compare these minimum numbers with the maximum total population numbers from 1991, from the census?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: And it was not a problem for you in making your report?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... I -- I think I don't understand you correctly. Comparing, meaning looking; or comparing, meaning analysing them? What do you mean by compare, did I compare? I produced, of course, certain numbers also on the population based on the voters' register, and they are in the report, in the annex of this case report. There are numbers of the voters, registered voters, overall sample size for every ethnic group, every municipality, and next to them there would be 1991 numbers. So in this sense the numbers are there in the report. But as I stressed earlier today, the absolute numbers for 1997 is not the overall population size so are not directly comparable with the overall population size in 1991. And this is what I'm saying again.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: I understand what you're saying. But you have to show some understanding for us as well. Most of us here in the courtroom are not experts in statistics or mathematics or your methods, and I'm trying to translate all this into layman's language to be able to understand, myself. As you've said more than once, in the voters' registers from 1997 there is no information about ethnicity, and you said you took over that information from the 1991 census using the method of comparison?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Now, scientifically speaking, can that then be then considered an independent source if you are using one source of information and then you graft onto it a portion from another source? Can we speak, in that case, about an independent source?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think the issue of independency of a source here is completely irrelevant. So these are two related sources that report on the same population largely. The voters' population is a subpopulation from the census. There is nothing wrong in matching these two sources and taking pieces of information from Source A and moving these pieces into Source B for the purpose of compiling statistics. There is absolutely no problem, statistical problem, or whatever other problem. And independence is completely irrelevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Very well. Now, as far as the estimates of population are concerned, would you agree that, on the one hand, we have 1991 population born before 1980, which means that in 1998 they would be of age, that means 18 and over.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see a question here.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Right. I will move on. This population born between -- born before 1980 imply that the figure from -- for 1991 includes all those people and also those who are under 18 but who could be voters in 1997 and 1998?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is what we did. We, from the town's population, took a subpopulation of people who later, in the future, as of 1997, for the first time would become eligible to vote. So it isn't a incomplete census population; that's correct. If it is your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Yes. And I have a follow-up question to this. Can you tell us, because it's not in the report, what is the population that, in 1991, was 18 and over, as opposed to the other portion of the population who could become voters later?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't say it from my head. I could calculate statistics. But this is irrelevant because the method we used in our study is a longitudinal method. That means longitudinal is following the same individuals over time. The same individuals over time. So the age of eligible voters in 1991, during the census, only matters from the point of view of whether or not they were eligible in 1997 to vote. So it is not that we have cross-section in 1991 of the population 18 plus and a cross-section of population 18 plus in 1997, we work with longitudinal data, as I said. We trace the same individual over time. So the age structure of this population of eligible voters in 1991 is not important. I can provide it with you, if you like to have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: If I may pick up on that, did you consider as potential voters in 1997 all those who, in 1991, were over 75 years old?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, there is no limit, age limit, for eligible voter. I mean, upper limit. But I guess, yeah, you might expect that elderly, the elderly, because of the health status or so, show less interest in voting, yes. But formally, there is no age limit, upper limit.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: I agree with you on that. But did you have any database on mortality that would enable to conclude out of the 1991 census how many people died a natural death between 1991 and 1997 and, therefore, could not be voters in 1997?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I have some information on natural death during the war. Not in 1996, not in 1997. And I do have records of war victims for entire country. It is approximately at least 90.000 deaths. So, most obviously dead, people don't vote; right? So it is not automatic that all people who were eligible to vote, according to the 1991 census, will be found as registered voters in 1997 elections. That is an obvious -- obvious observation, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: I think you said in chief that you received a database in 2004 on mortality. If you had had this data, if you had included it, would you also have been able to decrease the 1991 census by using the comparison method, the same way you did with the ethnicity of voters? In case I didn't make myself clear, I can -- if I understood your paper correctly, you take a voter registered to vote in 1997 and find him in the 1991 census and then you also take his nationality, his ethnicity, from there?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Couldn't you use the same method to find all those who died a natural death and exclude them as possible voters in 1997?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: If they are dead, they are not in the voters' list because they are dead. So it really is irrelevant. Well, the thing is that -- hmm. I don't think that that's matter in our assessment of the ethnic composition in 1991 or 1997. It -- they -- there is no bias whatsoever related to deaths or missing persons or whatever. Natural deaths, unnatural deaths, they don't matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: And to conclude this portion, the total of 1991 population includes people who were, in 1991, over 18, those who would be 18 and over in 1997, and unknown number of people who died between April 1992 and the elections in 1997; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the census population includes, of course, everybody who was living in Bosnia at the time of the census. Some of those who lived in Bosnia at that time died during the war of natural deaths. So that's the fact. This is all I can say.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: I think you've already said that in making this report you used some sources from Republika Srpska but not for 1993 and 1995. Did you, however, have the official statistics from the Republic Statistical Institute of RS about the total population in 1996 and 1997?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Hmm, I didn't have any statistics, population statistics, from the RS statistical authority for 1996 and 1997. And I think if they had some statistics on the population, these must have come from estimates, population projections, and not actual observed counts, as those from the population census.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: I agree with you absolutely. But I will also share with you that the estimates, in official statistics of RS, are that in Banja Luka there were a total population of 218.519; and in your report, we read the number of 86.456, although I see now that these are only people 18 and over. I apologise. So we'll move to something else. In your report, you said that all persons who left to work abroad before the war and who, in 1997, reported to vote from abroad, you treated them all as refugees. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: In your Milosevic report, where you explain your methodology, you say, on page 6 in B/C/S and in English, you say: "If the war had not broken out in Bosnia and Herzegovina, the pre-census emigres would have maybe returned. However, in 1997/1998, they registered as voters still living abroad. We therefore consider that all voters outside the country may and should be considered as refugees."

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Based on what relevant facts do you make this conclusion? Is there any statistical category to include wishes and intentions? How can you know what people would or would not have done? It's a subjective decision and choice, and you spoke about objectivity.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are right that I didn't study the intentions, return intentions, these kinds of things. However, I did study this issue from the statistical point of view. In the Milosevic report, there is a separate annex that is discussing exclusively the issue of the oversea population, as we call it, and the impact of this population being abroad at the time of the census on our statistics on IDPs and refugees and internally displaced persons. And this is annex, if I can direct your attention, it is Annex B4. It's Annex B4, which is extremely relevant to your question. So approximately there were 420.000, as far as I remember, individuals, 420.000 individuals, that are reported in the voters' register as the out-of-country voters. So the question is: What portion of this population left the country after the population census and what portion left the country before the population census? We studied this number and identified only 28.000 individuals, approximately, who left the country before the 1991 census. This is an extremely small portion of the entire population reported in the census, and, further, we are showing in this annex that the bias related to, including this one little group in our statistics, is negligible. It has practically no significant impact on our statistics on IDPs and refugees and ethnic composition. Well, there are, in statistics, two concepts of the population: The population call de facto and the population called de jure. De facto population is the population that actually lives in the territory of a country during the population census. And de jure population is the population that includes de facto population and, as well, individuals who temporarily stay abroad, that means are not saying physically in the country during the census. So Bosnia and Herzegovina and the entire former Yugoslavia was, as a matter of fact, known of a large group of people temporarily staying abroad. And this phenomenon started in the year 1970s, I believe, and continued still until the war broke out in the 1990s. So we compared the ethnic composition in the municipalities in Bosnia and Herzegovina for both de facto and de jure population. That means excluding and including the population temporarily staying abroad. And the result of this exercise is, as far as I remember, there were only two municipalities in which the ethnic composition would have been different, if instead of de jure population we analysed and based our statistics on de facto population. And these are only two municipalities out of 109 municipalities in the entire country. So that's the impact which could have been noted in our statistics. And -- I think I even estimated the error, the bias, which was less than 5 per cent. The usually accepted error in statistics. So if you like to go to Annex B4.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: No, no, no.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... in this annex, you can find a thorough explanation of your question, and my answer is there is no significant impact at all. And one important thing needs to be mentioned: That of these overall number of out-of-country voters, at least 100.000 individuals were travelling in the 1990s between their permanent residence in Bosnia and Herzegovina to workplaces in Croatia or Serbia. So they returned home weekly or even daily, a large portion of them daily. So as a matter of fact, well, we call them de jure population, but it is de facto population living in the same country. So that explains, I think, the essence of the problem. As a matter of fact, we can -- I cannot agree that the population temporarily staying abroad is a major issue that has impact on our statistics.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Bearing in mind that you just said that the entire territory of the former Yugoslavia was well known for these migrations, wherein in the 1950s and 1960s people left abroad en masse to work there, therefore, we cannot consider these migrations as consequences of war. That -- that part of the population could have been excluded. Perhaps for the purposes of your research it is not important, but for me ...

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I may comment here. To give you a good illustration of the scale of war-related migration, at the end of the war in Bosnia and Herzegovina, more than two million people were displaced or refugees. Basically UNHCR estimated it was 2.2 million people at the end of the war who were displaced, externally or internally. If you take into account the size of the population in 1991 which was 4.4 million, we are speaking of 50 per cent of people who became displaced internally or externally. If I say that this is a regular migration, educational for work, for family reunion or whatever, I'm sorry, I totally and completely disagree. So the war-related migration has other -- had other motivation and other underlying mechanics than the pre-war migration. That was mainly economical migration in the case of the Yugoslav people, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: I agree with that. But let us speak about something else. In your report about this, on page 5 in the last paragraph, you say -- and it's page 6 in Serbian and page 7 in English: "In order to integrate these two data sets," referring to the 1991 census and the 1997 voters' register, "we applied a complex matching procedure. In that procedure, the huge majority of persons entered in voters' registers, that is, about 80 per cent was found in the 1991 census." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Well, now, let us take a look at Table 1M. It's on page 30 of both the English and the Serbian versions.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] ... sorry, which report are we ...

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: The Milosevic report? Or the other one, the addendum? Oh, I see. For the case-specific report. My apologies. I misunderstood.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 65 ter 10399; that's page 30.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: You say that: "Inhabitants of all ethnicities in 1991 make up a total of 817.898, and you matched with -- to them 376.050 persons according to the data from 1997, which is 45.9 per cent." Can you explain what this is about?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can. This number, 376.000, approximately, is not the number of matched voters that can be directly related to the total of 817.898. Here, in this table, in Table 1, whether for Muslims or any other ethnic group, we present the ethnic composition and the fractions and sizes of the population as of 1991 and as of 1997. This is a snap-shot. That means that the population living in these municipalities in 1991 is shown, on one hand, and 1997, on the other hand. However, if you think a little bit, if you take the 1991 population and you look for these persons, how they moved during the war period and in the years after war until 1997, why would you expect to find them in exactly the same municipalities as shown in this table? So the thing is that this table is prepared according to the municipality of case study area; right? So the persons from Prijedor, for instance, that were in Prijedor, 94.000, all ethnicities, of which 40.000 Muslims, approximately, we read on page 30, 94.000, approximately, of all ethnicities, 40.000 of Muslims. Prijedor is one of the municipalities where extreme population movements took place. As we discussed earlier this morning, there were very large groups of Muslims that moved out from this municipality and ended in several other municipalities. These other municipalities being in the Federation, of course, not in the RS, as the case study area is defined. So the expectation that you would find them here under 1997, those originally reported in Prijedor as 40.000 is completely wrong. These are different people simply. Why? Because Muslims moved out, Serbs moved in. And the 1997 statistics does not give us the impression of the matched records that can be directly related to 1991 population from a given municipality but it gives the status as of 1997, which can be done. Which can be done based on the voters' register simply. But when we move to Table 2 where the IDPs are discussed, then we can compare the linked records, right, because then we look at the municipality of origin and how did they move to all other kinds of municipalities. So this is how the linking works.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: I was going to ask you just that. In all tables, marked as 2, let's take 2M. The item that's called "A Total Population Identified in 1991," you speak about 600-odd thousand, whereas there was a different figure elsewhere. Can you account for the difference? Is the difference due to the fact that the -- their whereabouts, that is, the municipality in Bosnia-Herzegovina where they were found, was disregarded, if I understood you correctly?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Excuse me, can we have Table 2 on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: If Your Honours please, just one thing arising out of that question. The witness is being asked to do a comparison, but we know part of what's being looked at for comparison purposes but not what else has to be looked at for comparison purposes. Mentioned "elsewhere." Do we know elsewhere, or what other table is being referred to?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From the previous answer, the witness spoke about tables marked 1. She explained in her previous answer how those figures in Table 1 came about, and in Tables -- Tables 1, that is, 1M, for example, we see population sample from 1997, all, that is, all ethnicities, it says 376.050. And here in Table 2 we see total population 1997, all, 439.000 and something. Can you explain, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the Judge, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Sorry. We are looking for page 2 -- table 2. We need a page number.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 38.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: It starts on 37, so if -- are we to look at the -- at page 38 in the English or 37? Just curious.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: We seem to have it now on the screen, Table 2M.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: May I start answering? Yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think, first of all, I would like to clarify that the tables in Annex A, whether A1, A2, or A3, cannot be used in order to obtain the exact matching rates. That is one thing. Second, I want to clarify that in these tables there will be two types of the population numbers presented. The first type is the so-called population in, as I call it, and the other time we will speak about the population from. In and from population. What does it mean in and from population? Well, it's good to realize that in the analysis of migration there are always two perspectives. The municipality of origin or place of origin, region of origin; and the municipality or place of destination. So my migration is a two-dimensional process. And this, in some extent, is to be seen in this results presented in Annex A. So in annex A there is one perspective, the in perspective. That means -- well, the listing of municipalities is exactly as in the indictment. This is the municipalities of the origin of the population. So for 1991, we have the census figure. That was the population in these municipalities in 1991. Then we move further, and we look at the 1997 sample population, and it is again the in population. So the population that was observed in the same municipalities, municipalities of origin, in 1997. These are two snap-shots. It is very important to realize that the 1997 in population will be composed of several parts. One part will be people who didn't move. They stayed. They just remained in the same municipalities. But there will be newcomers as well, and that won't be listed here because they are gone; right? Moreover, it is a sample. It is a sample population. It is the voters' register. So those who did not register to vote are not here, are not reported. And those who are not matched are not reported either, because we have this analysis done by ethnicity. So this is why I have been repeating all the time: Don't take the 1997 population absolute numbers as the size of the population in 1997. As a matter of fact, these are two cross-sections, two snap-shots: One is 1991 one is 1997. The population that lived in. So in 1991 there was a certain ethnic make-up, and then we move to 1997 and this is what we observe, if we compile our individual data according to the municipality as in the indictment. And now we move to Table 2. So the in and from population are not the same. So these numbers cannot be ever the same, you see?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: I apologise. Let me ask you something. Did I understand you correctly, when we speak about the figure from Table 1, that is, 376.050 persons, we're talking about identified persons who in these 18 municipalities registered as voters in 1997; and when we speak about the 439.601 persons, we're talking about all identified persons who live in these 18 municipalities or hail from one of them, no matter in which municipality of Bosnia-Herzegovina you were able to find them in 1997, as registered voters? Did I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, in 1997, we have the people who registered to vote in 1997 in these municipalities. In these municipalities. So if you go to Prijedor, to illustrate my statement, for Muslims we have a very small number, 397. This is a sample of Muslims who registered in Prijedor to vote in the 1997 election. This is the meaning of snap-shot. This -- so this is the in population in 1991 and in 1997. Disregarding the place of origin, this is the number of Muslims who registered to vote in 1997 in Prijedor. 397.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Can we have the next page on the screen, please, with the Prijedor municipality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So it is the table at page 38.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: So, Madam Witness, could you -- could you please explain all the figures, the numbers that are there with regard to Prijedor, with regard to what you just explained?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Table 2 is a little bit more complex because here we look at the municipality of origin. So Prijedor are all those who, in the census, registered in Prijedor, and we identified in 1997 49.019 Muslims in all kinds of municipalities. In all kinds of municipalities. 49.019.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: So that's people that are still living in Prijedor or living elsewhere within Bosnia-Herzegovina --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: -- but hailing from Prijedor, coming from Prijedor in 1991?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... thank you. For the 49.000.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... yes, that's correct. In Prijedor or elsewhere in Bosnia or out of country, if the person was a refugee. So this is the longitudinal character of this statistic; right? So that many were there in the voters' register from Prijedor from 1991, in all kinds of places. So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: I would have like to have the other numbers explained as well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Well, this is the total population. Sorry, I was speaking of Muslim population, but in the first column it is the total population. So in the next panel, it is the Muslim population. Sorry. Sorry. So the first three columns is the total population identified in 1997, so it is all ethnicities. But in the next three columns, it is the Muslim population identified in 1997.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Sorry, the three first columns --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: -- are total -- total population of --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of Prijedor. Of Prijedor. All ethnicities. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: And what is 21.964, then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is the IDPs and refugees among them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... and the percentage --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- next percentage, how many was it. The 21.964.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: The percentage of the refugees?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In all ethnicities. All ethnicities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And the next three columns, it's exactly the same numbers only for Muslims. For just one ethnic group. So we have 19.658 of Muslims from Prijedor in 1991 identified in all kinds of places, and of these 19.658 there were as many as 19.290 IDPs and refugees, which is 98.1 per cent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That explains the little number in Table 1 for Muslims who registered in Prijedor to vote in 1997 elections. So there is -- these are two different, obviously, two completely different types of population figures, and you cannot relate them and say we are inconsistent because this number is different than that number. These numbers tell us two different things. Table 1 tell us about the ethnic composition as identified in 1991, 1997. Table 2 is meant for a totally different purpose. It is meant to tell us how many persons, in relative terms as percentages, became displaced as 1997/1998. So as of 1997/1998 they are still not living at their 1991 place of residence. That's the point. So these are two completely different tables.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: I understood what you said, but let us take a look at Table 1S on page 37 in the Serbian and page 36 in the English. In line 1, column 5, we see 1997 sample population, and it says that there's a total of 271.209 Serbs. Have you found it?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think you are speaking of the entire area; right? 271.209; right? The entire area. Yes, yes, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: I apologise if I was imprecise. Table 2S, on page 39 -- actually, it will -- it's probably another page that. It should be 45. I apologise. Yes. And now here again for the entire area, line 1, column 4, we see Serb population identified in 1997, all, and the number is 216.009.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, again, you are comparing what is incomparable. These are two different populations, sir. This number, 216.000, is according to the municipality of origin. That would be the study case area as such and found anywhere, anywhere, in Bosnia or outside it. Which is different from the first number, the 271.000, which is giving the number of Serbs in this particular area. Again, in and from. In and from. Two different numbers. We don't compare them because it is wrong to compare them. Sorry, migration is a complex phenomenon. People move starting from the place of origin, and they go to different places and arrive at their destination at some point, and on their way they stay in all kinds of other place. So migration is a multi-dimensional process, and that is seen in our statistics.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: I believe when you when you say it is a multi-dimensional process, but where I want to deal with other things here, so we need explanations. Let us return to Table 1S, therefore, which is on page 37 in the Serbian and page 36 in the English. I'm interested in some percentages. You said that in 1991 Serbs accounted for 44.7 per cent of the overall population, the population that was of age. And in 1997, the percentage was 72.1 per cent. Please explain that. Because, to my mind, the share of Serbs rose by 27.4 per cent, rather than by 61.3. If we're talking about shares. It may be amusing to you, but I show you I said goodbye to math long ago. Could you please explain.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it is higher, perhaps, by these number of per cent points that you mentioned, but it does not express the overall change in this per cent; right? So it is -- the 61.3 is the so-called relative difference. So if you take an absolute difference between 44.7 and 72.1 and then divide this difference by the initial 44.7, then you obtain the change -- change in the percentages. I think one of the Defence experts raised this issue and was also confused about it, but one has to be careful. So the increase or decline expressed as an absolute difference between two percentages is a wrong measure of the change. It doesn't show the actual character of the change. I must disappoint you, my measure is correct statistically and not yours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Fortunately, I chose another job to do in life and not statistics. That was a joke, of course. I have some questions about internally displaced persons that you mention in your reports. Even today, in the examination-in-chief, you made mention of them. The Milosevic report, on page 8, paragraph 3, in the Serbian; or page 7, last paragraph in English, you say: "Note that our definitions of internally displaced persons and refugees are statistical not legal." And you mentioned as much today. Could you please repeat the statistical definition of IDPs and refugees.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said earlier today, we compared places of where people resided in 1991 and at the time of election, which was expressed in the voters' register in the variable called the municipality of registration and the registration centre. As a matter of fact, there exists a legal definition of an internally displaced person or a refugee. This definition involves a certain fear that a person experienced because of being persecuted due to all kinds of reasons, including the ethnicity, for instance, religion, language, nationality and others. These legal definitions are used by organisations like UNHCR and by governments when registering people as internally displaced persons and refugees. In order to be registered, one has to fulfill a certain legal criteria, including this fear element of being persecuted, for certain reasons. And once a person is registered, the person is entitled to certain benefits. To financial aid, for instance, material aid, accommodation is provided, et cetera, et cetera. We, of course, did not, could not use this kind of definition because it is not in our data. And, as a matter of fact, well, I think it was not fully available even to the UNHCR and the -- the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina. In our statistics, we used a statistical definition, that is, the comparison of the actual place of residence in 1991 and 1997. It was the municipality of residence in both cases. If it was different in 1997 from 1991, we assumed, we took such a case as a case of displaced person. The place was in Bosnia but different than 1991 for internally displaced persons, and it was outside Bosnia in 1997 for persons whom we considered refugees. So a refugee also in the legal definition is a person who left his or her own country and moved to other countries. And internally displaced persons stayed within the borders of a country but doesn't live anymore in his or her original place of residence. So we didn't use the legal definition. We used the statistical definitions.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, there are only a couple of minutes left, but I would like to move onto another topic. And I would like to take the opportunity to take another look at the transcript and possibly reduce the scope of my cross-examination that's left. So I would, therefore, suggest to stop here. And I can continue tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes. So we take the adjournment to 9.00 tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: The -- I remind counsel that -- of the extended sitting tomorrow. We will be back in this courtroom for the 2.30-to-4.00 sitting tomorrow afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Aleksic, how much time do you expect that you would need when we resume tomorrow morning?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, maybe another hour. But I really cannot be certain. It may be less than that, actually.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 7th day of October, 2010, at 9.00 a.m.
